Module io.github.brantunger.unruly.core
Package io.github.brantunger.unruly.api

Class RulesEngineBuilder<O>

java.lang.Object
io.github.brantunger.unruly.api.RulesEngineBuilder<O>
Type Parameters:
O - The type of the output object
public final class RulesEngineBuilder<O> extends Object
Configures and builds a RulesEngine. An engine's languages, imports, listeners, limit on compiled copies, copies made at load, run timeout and clock are set here and can't change once it's built; only its rules can, with RulesEngine.load(List).

Compiled copies: a run uses a copy of the rules that no other run is using, and an engine keeps as many as the most runs it has had in progress at once. A thread pool bounds that; virtual threads don't, so by default an engine limits runs on virtual threads to one copy for every two processors. maxCopies(int) sets a limit for every kind of thread, and unlimitedCopies() turns it off, leaving only build slots to pace new copies on virtual threads. See Compiled copies. 

RulesEngine<LoanDecision> engine = RulesEngineBuilder.firstMatch(LoanDecision::new)
        .imports("java.time")
        .listener(new LoggingRuleListener())
        .build();
engine.load(rules);

Languages: an engine built without language(ExpressionLanguage) has the languages found with ServiceLoader, such as MVEL from the unruly-engine artifact. An engine built with it has exactly the languages given. A rule whose language is null is written in the engine's default language: the one named with defaultLanguage(String), or else the engine's only language.

A builder isn't thread-safe. build() can be called more than once, and each call builds a new engine with the settings at that moment.

  • Method Details

    • firstMatch

      public static <O> RulesEngineBuilder<O> firstMatch(Supplier<O> outputFactory)
      Starts building an engine that fires the action of the highest-priority rule whose condition is true: the first match, in DMN's terms. Rules with equal priorities keep their list order.

      Conditions are evaluated in that order, and the run stops at the first match, so the rules below it are never evaluated: they're neither matched nor unmatched, the run's result reports them as not evaluated, and a broken condition among them can't fail a run that's already decided. Use allMatches(Supplier) or uniqueMatch(Supplier) when every condition must be evaluated. A rule the run skips is never evaluated, and is reported as skipped wherever it is; see Rule.

      Type Parameters:
      O - The type of the output object
      Parameters:
      outputFactory - Creates the output object. It is called once per run that matches a rule and must return a new, non-null object each time.
      Returns:
      A new builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if outputFactory is null

    • uniqueMatch

      public static <O> RulesEngineBuilder<O> uniqueMatch(Supplier<O> outputFactory)
      Starts building an engine that fires the action of the one rule whose condition is true, and fails the run when more than one is: DMN's unique match, for a decision table whose rows must not overlap. Every condition, except those of rules the run skips, is evaluated, in priority order, before anything fires, so the failure names every rule that matched.

      No match returns null, like the other engines. More than one match fires nothing, doesn't call the output supplier, and throws a RuleExecutionException that names each matched rule in priority order and belongs to no rule: listeners get afterEvaluate for every rule the run doesn't skip, then onRunError. It depends on nothing language-specific: it counts the conditions that were true.

      Type Parameters:
      O - The type of the output object
      Parameters:
      outputFactory - Creates the output object. It is called once per run that matches exactly one rule and must return a new, non-null object each time.
      Returns:
      A new builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if outputFactory is null

    • imports

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> imports(String... names)
      Adds imports that every language compiles rules with, so rule expressions can refer to classes by their simple names. Each string is a fully qualified package name ("java.util") or class name ("java.time.LocalDate", or "java.util.Map.Entry" for a nested class). A language without imports ignores them.

      Whether a string names a class is decided by build(), with the building thread's context class loader, or this library's class loader if the thread has none. A string that loader doesn't find as a class, but that is a valid package name, is imported as a package. Classes in imported packages are looked up each time rules are loaded, with the loading thread's context class loader.

      Parameters:
      names - Package or class names
      Returns:
      This builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if names or any element is null; nothing is added

    • fact

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> fact(String name, Class<?> type)
      Declares a fact's name and type, so the engine checks a run's value against the type and a language can check its expressions against it.

      The engine fails a run with IllegalArgumentException when the fact is present and its value isn't an instance of type. A null value passes: nothing about it contradicts the declaration. A run that doesn't supply the fact at all is unaffected, unless requireDeclaredFacts() is also set. Declaring a fact twice replaces the first declaration.

      A primitive type is declared as its wrapper, so fact("age", int.class) accepts an Integer, and languages are told Integer. RulesEngine.load(List) checks every declared name with the language of each rule, as a run checks the names it's given, so a name no language can refer to fails loading rather than every run.

      Languages are told what was declared, and use it as they can, for example to check their expressions when the rules load; the engine's own check happens whatever the language does. See each language's documentation.

      Parameters:
      name - The fact's name, as rules refer to it
      type - The type a run's value must be an instance of. Declaring Object or a Map says the fact's shape isn't fixed, which no language can type-check
      Returns:
      This builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if name or type is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if name is output, which actions use for the output object

    • requireDeclaredFacts

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> requireDeclaredFacts()
      Rejects a run that supplies a fact nobody declared, or leaves a declared fact out. Without this, declaring a fact only says what its type is when it's there.

      It says that fact(String, Class) lists every fact a run may supply, which is what lets a language reject an expression that refers to anything else, when the language offers that and it's turned on: for MVEL, its strongTyping option, which also needs this. The engine's own checks on a run's facts don't depend on any language.

      Returns:
      This builder

    • maxCopies

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> maxCopies(int maxCopies)
      Keeps at most maxCopies compiled copies of the rules, for runs on every kind of thread, instead of the default limit on runs from virtual threads.

      A run that starts while all of them are in use waits until one is free, so at most maxCopies runs make progress at once. A run started from inside another run on the same thread, and a run that has waited five seconds without one single copy being given back, don't wait: each gets an extra copy that isn't kept. A run that is interrupted while it waits, or that passes its deadline there, throws a RuleExecutionException; an interrupted thread keeps its interrupt status set. A rule list whose languages all return Session.none() needs no copies, and no limit applies to it.

      Parameters:
      maxCopies - The most compiled copies of the rules to keep, and so the most runs making progress at once; at least 1
      Returns:
      This builder
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if maxCopies is less than 1
      See Also:
      • Limiting the copies

    • unlimitedCopies

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> unlimitedCopies()
      Makes as many compiled copies of the rules as the runs in progress need, on any kind of thread, instead of the default limit on runs from virtual threads.

      Like an engine before 2.0, its runs never wait for a copy, which suits a thread pool, whose size bounds the copies. On a virtual thread, a run that finds no idle copy, and isn't nested in another run on that thread, first waits for one of the engine's build slots, one for each processor, and holds it until the new copy's first run ends, which is when a language such as MVEL compiles the expressions. The slots pace the new copies without bounding them: the copies still grow with the runs in progress, so rules that wait — on I/O, a database or another service — can make many. In a language such as MVEL, each copy recompiles every expression and generates its own accessor classes. For a hard bound, use maxCopies(int) sized for the runs you want waiting at once; with MVEL on JDK 21 to 23, below the number of carriers, since a limit at or above it can deadlock every carrier there, and so can this.

      A run with a deadline waits for a slot for at most half the time it has left, and a run that sees no slot given back for five seconds stops waiting; either then makes its copy without a slot, so no run fails for want of a copy. A run interrupted while it waits throws a RuleExecutionException, and its thread keeps its interrupt status set. Runs on platform threads never wait.

      Returns:
      This builder
      See Also:
      • Waiting for a build slot

    • copiesAtLoad

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> copiesAtLoad(int count)
      Makes count compiled copies of the rules each time RulesEngine.load(List) runs, so the first runs borrow copies that are ready instead of making them. Without this, no copy is made until a run needs one.

      Making a copy compiles the rules again, in each language that keeps state between runs, and prepares its sessions with warmUp: MVEL compiles every condition and action into it. load() makes the copies one after another on its own thread, after compiling the rules and before runs can see them, so runs go on using the rules it replaces meanwhile, and load() takes that much longer. For example, 16 copies of 21 MVEL rules added about 65 ms to a reload that otherwise took 15 ms. Rules whose languages all keep no state between runs get one set of sessions that every run shares, whatever count is.

      It's for runs on virtual threads on JDK 24 and later, where a run that makes a copy can keep its carrier while MVEL loads the classes it compiles. It doesn't stop MVEL generating accessor classes during a copy's first runs, and a copy made during a run, such as one for a run nested in another, is made as before. See Class loading pins carriers.

      Parameters:
      count - How many copies to make; zero, the default, makes none. With maxCopies(int), it can't be more than the limit, since no more copies than that are used at once. The default limit, on runs from virtual threads only, and unlimitedCopies() allow any number.
      Returns:
      This builder
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if count is negative; build() throws it if count is more than maxCopies(int)

    • runTimeout

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> runTimeout(Duration timeout)
      Stops a run that is still going after timeout. Without this, a run has no deadline.

      The deadline is taken from when RulesEngine.run(FactStore) is called, and waiting for a compiled copy of the rules counts towards it. The engine checks it before each condition and each action, and again when each one returns, so a run whose last condition or action returns past its deadline fails even though that rule finished. It doesn't stop an expression that is already running; only a language that checks EvaluationContext.isCancelled() can stop inside one. A run past its deadline throws a RuleExecutionException caused by a TimeoutException.

      Parameters:
      timeout - How long a run may take; positive. RunOptions.withTimeoutOf(Duration) gives a single run one instead.
      Returns:
      This builder
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if timeout is zero or negative
      NullPointerException - if timeout is null
      See Also:
      • Stopping a run

    • clock

      public RulesEngineBuilder<O> clock(Clock clock)
      Sets the clock a run reads, once when it starts, to decide which rules are within their validity window (Rule.getValidFrom(), Rule.getValidTo()). Without this, the engine uses Clock.systemUTC(). A test can give a fixed clock, such as Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2027-06-01T00:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC), to run the rules as they're scheduled at that time.

      Only the validity window uses the clock. A run timeout is measured with the system clock whatever clock is set here. Anything the clock throws fails the run unchanged, before any listener is told the run started; a null instant fails it the same way, with a NullPointerException.

      The instant a run read is its RunContext.startedAt(), which listeners get, and its RunResult.startedAt(), so an audit record can say what time judged the windows.

      Parameters:
      clock - The clock
      Returns:
      This builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if clock is null

    • build

      public RulesEngine<O> build()
      Builds an engine with this builder's settings. Load its rules with RulesEngine.load(List) before the first run.
      Returns:
      A new engine
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the engine has no expression language; if it has several and no default language; if the default language, or a language given an option, isn't one of its languages; or if a language found with ServiceLoader has a null or blank name, or two found languages have the same name. Anything ServiceLoader or a language throws while it's found, such as a ServiceConfigurationError, is thrown unchanged.
      IllegalArgumentException - if an import is neither a loadable class nor a valid package name, or names a class that exists but can't be loaded, for example because a class it depends on is missing; or if copiesAtLoad(int) is more than maxCopies(int)
